(may use /). When a work has no entry, build-work-page.mjs emits its generic paragraph. Curated prose lives HERE, never only in generated site HTML — rebuilds must be safe.
9741: Abbo, abbot of Fleury, addressed this collection of canons to Hugh Capet and his son Robert about 995–996 — a mirror of royal duty and a defense of the monastic order, stitched from councils, the Theodosian code, and the fathers. The Latin is Migne's printing (PL 139, coll. 473A–508A), from the Corpus Corporum transcription; Migne's text descends from the early modern editions and prints fifty-two chapters, where the one complete manuscript carries forty-four. Parenthetical references in small type stand on Migne's page — editorial identifications inherited from the edition he reprinted or supplied by his shop, not Abbo's; the author's own citations run in the prose itself. Every gilt column mark is an address: migne.app/pl/139/473a resolves to the first.
7561: The Commonitorium — a title best rendered 'reminder' or 'memorandum' — was written on the island of Lérins about 434 by the monk Vincent, who signs himself Peregrinus, the Pilgrim. It is the classic Western statement of how the Church holds its faith across time: the catholic rule is what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all (quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est), and doctrine grows only as a body grows, developing without ever becoming something other than itself. Migne prints the surviving first book together with the recapitulation that is all that remains of the lost second (PL 50, coll. 637C–686B), from the Corpus Corporum transcription of Baluze's edition. This is not the first English of the Commonitorium — it has been translated before, notably by C. A. Heurtley in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers and by Rudolph Morris in the Fathers of the Church — and we make no claim otherwise. We render it afresh because a text this central to how the tradition understands itself belongs in migne.app's own voice, set beside its Latin column for column. The gilt marks carry Migne's numbering: migne.app/pl/50/637 resolves to the opening.
7383: This short exposition of the Magnificat — Mary's canticle from the first chapter of Luke — comes down without an author's name. Migne prints it among the appendix of works gathered under Augustine's name but not by him (PL 40, coll. 1137–1142), where much of the pseudo-Augustinian and anonymous material of the tradition was collected; the Latin here is the Corpus Corporum transcription of that printing. We render it as it stands, anonymous, letting the text speak for itself. The gilt column marks carry Migne's own numbering: migne.app/pl/40/1137 resolves to the opening.
11545: Migne prints this under Richard's name, but it is two texts. The dedicatory letter that opens it (cols. 1011–1013A) is Richard's, and it announces an exposition of Psalm 118:135 — «Illumina faciem tuam» — that never follows. Richard's actual exposition of that verse stands separately in the same volume, at PL 196, 346–354, where it begins abruptly with no dedication at all: the two are halves of one work, parted in Migne's arrangement. What occupies the rest of these columns (1013A–1018C) is a different piece altogether, a sermon on the baptism of Christ. It is generally assigned to Walter of Saint Victor, Richard's successor as prior, and the internal grounds are suggestive — its attack on those who say «Christus non est aliquid inquantum est homo» is the charge of Christological nihilianism that Walter levelled at Peter Lombard, in the register for which he is remembered. But we have not been able to trace that attribution to a published argument, and record it here rather than in the byline for that reason.
pg:joel-chronographia: Of Joel nothing is known but this book: a world chronicle in brief, from Adam to the taking of Constantinople by the crusaders in 1204, at which it breaks off with a cry — and these things Christians did to Christians. The Greek is Migne's printing (PG 139, coll. 224–288), which reprints Leo Allatius's 1651 edition with his Latin version in the facing column; our text rests on the Calfa–GREgORI optical transcription of the volume, corrected against the plates where the printer let a Greek line stray into the Latin column (three such restorations, each verified on the scan). The chronicle garbles history freely — kings conflated, reigns misnumbered — and the translation preserves every such reading; it translates what Migne prints. Each gilt column number is an address: migne.app/pg/139/224 resolves to the first.
pg:antiochus-epistula-ad-eustathium: Antiochus was a monk of the Great Laura of Saint Sabas in the Judaean desert. In this letter he answers Eustathius, abbot of Attalina near Ancyra in Galatia, who had written asking two things: for an abridgement of Scripture he could carry while displaced, and for the truth about reports he had heard concerning the Laura's monks. The first request produced the Pandectes; this letter is its preface, and its second half is the answer to the second question — an account, from someone who arrived days afterwards, of the killing of the fathers of Mar Saba by raiders one week before Jerusalem fell in 614. It names the dead as forty-four, gives their feast as the fifteenth of May, and closes with a list of the burned sanctuaries of Jerusalem that Modestus was then rebuilding. On the text. PG 89 is one of the 128 Migne Greek volumes with no existing optical transcription, so unlike our other Greek works this text does not rest on the Calfa–GREgORI corpus. The Greek was established here by machine transcription of Migne's plates at 400 dpi, then checked word by word against an independent transcription of a second physical copy of the volume — two copies of one edition fail differently, and their disagreements locate the errors. All 1,178 words were read against the plate; every divergence between the two copies was resolved by hand and none proved to be a misreading of ours. Migne's parallel Latin column was consulted as a witness, with one caution the editor himself supplies: at the foot of column 1421 he admits that where this narrative was corrupt he often rendered it into Latin by conjecture, so his Latin cannot independently confirm the Greek. Where the two columns assert different facts the disagreement is marked in the translation rather than silently resolved. Each gilt column number is an address: migne.app/pg/89/1421 resolves to the first.
